# A. All-Pairs Cut Queries

## How to find it

Represent all pair minimum cuts by minimum edges on Gomory--Hu tree paths.

## Correctness

Residual cut-side reparenting preserves the tree-cut invariant at every construction step; path minima therefore equal original pair cuts.

## Complexity

The reference follows the standard polynomial bound of the named augmentation, flow, or contraction algorithm; explicit problem limits keep oracle-based matroid intersection practical.

The construction performs exactly `n-1` maximum-flow computations. Querying a
pair by walking its tree path is `O(n)` here; binary lifting can reduce this to
`O(log n)` when the query count requires it. The residual reachable side, not
the set of edges used by the flow, determines reparenting.

# B. Rainbow Forest

## How to find it

Intersect the graphic matroid with the color partition matroid.

## Correctness

Every exchange-path flip preserves both independences and grows the set; absence of a path certifies maximum cardinality.

## Complexity

The reference follows the standard polynomial bound of the named augmentation, flow, or contraction algorithm; explicit problem limits keep oracle-based matroid intersection practical.

With independence rebuilt directly for every tested exchange, the reference
is deliberately polynomial rather than asymptotically optimal. Under these
limits that keeps both oracles auditable. Exhaustive subset enumeration is the
recommended tiny-instance oracle.

# C. Dual Forest

## How to find it

Use two DSU forest oracles on different endpoint maps.

## Correctness

This is exactly two-matroid intersection, so the final common independent set is maximum.

## Complexity

The reference follows the standard polynomial bound of the named augmentation, flow, or contraction algorithm; explicit problem limits keep oracle-based matroid intersection practical.

Each graphic oracle is a DSU cycle test. Remember that the same selectable
element has two different endpoint pairs; using one DSU state for both maps
would test the wrong independence system.

# D. Directed Arborescence

## How to find it

Select minimum incoming edges, contract their directed cycles, and subtract those minima from crossing costs.

## Correctness

Every solution pays the accumulated minima and replaces exactly one entry per contracted cycle; reduced costs preserve the remaining choice.

## Complexity

The reference follows the standard polynomial bound of the named augmentation, flow, or contraction algorithm; explicit problem limits keep oracle-based matroid intersection practical.

The dense Chu--Liu/Edmonds implementation is `O(VE)`. Before contracting, fail
if a non-root component has no incoming edge. When an edge enters a contracted
cycle at vertex `v`, subtract the minimum incoming cost already charged for
`v`; this is the exact extra replacement cost.

# What to verify independently

For cut trees, compute a fresh max flow for every vertex pair on very small
graphs and compare it with every tree-path minimum. For matroid problems,
enumerate subsets and test both independence predicates. For arborescences,
enumerate one incoming edge per non-root vertex and retain only selections
reachable from the root. Parallel edges, zero capacities, directed cycles,
and unreachable vertices should all appear in the stress generator.
